questions.title: Coaching a Junior Candidate Through a C++ Coding Interview Debrief
questions.prompt: A junior engineer on your team is about to interview for a quant developer role that tests C++ fundamentals, and asks you to run a mock interview and give feedback. What do you focus the feedback on, beyond just 'right or wrong answer'?
questions.modelAnswer: I'd focus most of the feedback on how they communicated their reasoning while solving the problem, not just whether the final answer was correct, because that's usually the actual gap between a candidate who solved the problem and one who gets the offer -- interviewers are evaluating thought process as much as the result, and a candidate who silently stares and then produces a correct answer gives the interviewer much less to go on than one who narrates their reasoning as they go, including false starts. I'd specifically watch for whether they explained pointer-vs-reference and stack-vs-heap tradeoffs precisely when they came up naturally in the problem, rather than reciting a memorized definition disconnected from the actual code they were writing -- a correct recitation that doesn't connect to the specific line of code in front of them reads as rehearsed rather than understood. I'd also give feedback on how they handled not immediately knowing something: did they guess confidently and move on, or did they say 'I'm not sure, let me reason through it' and actually reason through it out loud -- the second is almost always the better interview behavior, since it shows genuine problem-solving under uncertainty rather than either false confidence or freezing. Finally, I'd point out any moment where recognizing a known problem pattern (a running-value, single-pass approach, for instance) would have shortened their path to a solution, since recognizing the shape of a problem is a skill that generalizes far more than memorizing any one specific solution, and that's the kind of feedback that actually improves their next interview, not just this one.
questions.professionalAnswer: Most of what I'd focus feedback on is the thinking-out-loud part, not just whether the final code was right -- interviewers are watching the reasoning as much as the result, and someone who narrates their process, including the false starts, usually comes across better than someone who goes quiet and eventually produces a correct answer. I'd specifically listen for whether concepts like pointers-vs-references or stack-vs-heap came up connected to the actual code in front of them, versus a recited definition that doesn't land anywhere specific -- the second reads as memorized, not understood. And I'd pay attention to how they handled not knowing something in the moment -- saying 'I'm not sure, let me think through it' and actually doing that is almost always better than guessing confidently or freezing. If there was a moment where recognizing a familiar problem pattern would have gotten them there faster, I'd point that out too, since that's a skill that transfers to the next interview, not just this one.
commonMistakes: Giving feedback only on whether the final answer was correct, not on the reasoning process
Not distinguishing a memorized, recited definition from one genuinely connected to the code at hand
Not addressing how the candidate handled moments of uncertainty during the problem
keyPoints: Feedback should focus on communicated reasoning, not just the final correctness of the answer
Watch for recited definitions disconnected from the actual code versus genuine, connected understanding
Handling uncertainty by reasoning aloud is better interview behavior than confident guessing or freezing
Pointing out recognizable problem patterns builds a transferable skill, not just a one-off answer

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly focuses feedback on communicated reasoning, not just correctness
Correctly distinguishes recited vs. genuinely connected understanding
Addresses handling of uncertainty during the interview
Notes the value of recognizing transferable problem patterns
